## 2

## Predictive Models in Data Structures:

## The Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter

Bloom filters are space-efficient probabilistic data structures used to test whether an element is a

member of a set20. A Bloom filter compresses a given set S into an array of bits. A Bloom filter may

allow false positives but will not give false-negative matches, which makes them suitable for numer-

ous memory-constrained applications in networks, databases, and other systems areas. Indeed, many

5


<!-- Page 16 -->


thousands of papers describe applications of Bloom filters26,34,40.

There is a trade-off between the false positive rate and the size of a Bloom filter (a lower false pos-

itive rate leads to a larger memory footprint). For a given false positive rate, there are known theo-

retical lower bounds on the space used by the Bloom filter93. However, these lower bounds assume

the Bloom filter could store any possible set. If the data set or the membership queries have a spe-

cific structure, it may be possible to beat the lower bounds in practice27,85,89. In particular, Kraska

et al.70 and Mitzenmacher86 propose using machine learning models to reduce the space further by

using a learned model to provide a suitable pre-filter for the membership queries. This allows one

to beat the space lower bounds by leveraging the context-specific information in the learned model.

Rae et al.98 propose a neural Bloom Filter that learns to write to memory using a distributed write

scheme and achieves compression gains over the classical Bloom filter.

The key idea of learned Bloom filters is that in many practical settings, given a query input, the

likelihood that the input is in the set S can be deduced by some observable features that a machine

learning model can capture. For example, a Bloom filter representing a set of malicious URLs can

benefit from a learned model that can distinguish malicious URLs from benign URLs. This model

can be trained on URL features such as the length of the hostname and the count of special charac-

ters. This approach is described by Kraska et al.70 in their study of how standard index structures

can be improved using machine learning models; we refer to their framework as the original learned

Bloom filter. Given an input x and its features, the model outputs a score s(x), which is supposed

to correlate with the likelihood of the input being in the set. Thus, the elements of the set, or keys,

should have a higher score value than non-keys. This model is used as a pre-filter, so when score s(x)

of an input x is above a pre-determined threshold t, it is directly classified as being in the set. For

inputs where s(x) < t, a smaller backup Bloom filter built from only keys with a score below the

threshold (which are known) is used. This maintains the property that there are no false negatives.

The design uses the model to immediately answer for inputs with high scores, whereas the rest of

6


<!-- Page 17 -->


the inputs are handled by the backup Bloom filter as shown in Figure 2.1A. The threshold value t

partitions the score space into two regions, and inputs are processed differently depending on which

region their score falls in. With a sufficiently accurate model, the size of the backup Bloom filter can

be significantly reduced compared to a standard Bloom filter while maintaining overall accuracy.

Kraska et al.70 showed that, in some applications, even after considering the model’s size, the learned

Bloom filter can be smaller than the standard Bloom filter for the same false positive rate.

The original learned Bloom filter compares the model score against a single threshold, but the

framework has several drawbacks.

Choosing the right threshold: Choosing the threshold value for the learned Bloom filter is

critical, but the original design uses heuristics to determine the threshold value.

Using more partitions: Comparing the score value only against a single threshold value wastes

information provided by the learning model. For instance, two elements x1, x2 with s(x1) >>

s(x2) > t are treated the same way, but the odds of x1 being a key are much higher than for x2. Intu-

itively, we should be able to do better by partitioning the score space into more than two regions.

Optimal Bloom filters for each region: Elements with scores above the threshold are directly

accepted as keys. A more general design would provide backup Bloom filters in both regions and

choose each region’s Bloom filter false positive rate to optimize the space/false positive trade-off as

desired. The original setup can be interpreted as using a Bloom filter of size 0 and a false positive rate

of 1 above the threshold. This may not be the optimal choice; moreover, as we show, using different

Bloom filters for each region (as shown in Figure 2.1C) allows further gains when we increase the

number of partitions.

Follow-up work by Mitzenmacher86 and Dai and Shrivastava33 improve the original design but

only address a subset of these drawbacks. In particular, Mitzenmacher86 proposes using Bloom fil-

ters for both regions, referred to as sandwiching, and provides a method to find the optimal false

positive rates for each Bloom filter. However, sandwiching only considers two regions and does not

7


<!-- Page 18 -->


consider how to find the optimal threshold value. For their Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ad-

aBF), Dai and Shrivastava33 propose using multiple thresholds to divide the space of scores into

multiple regions, with a different backup Bloom filter for each score region; however, the false pos-

itive rates for each of the backup Bloom filters and the threshold values are chosen using heuristics.

Empirically, we found that these heuristics might perform worse than the sandwiching method in

some scenarios.

A general design that resolves all the drawbacks would, given a target false positive rate and the

learned model, partition the score space into multiple regions with separate backup Bloom filters for

each region and find the optimal threshold values and false-positive rates under the goal of minimiz-

ing the memory usage while achieving the desired false positive rate as shown in Figure 2.1C. In this

work, we show how to frame this problem as an optimization problem and that our resulting solu-

tion significantly outperforms the heuristics used in previous works. Additionally, we show that our

maximum space saving* is linearly proportional to the KL divergence of the key and non-key score

distributions determined by the partitions. We present a dynamic programming algorithm to find

the optimal parameters (up to the discretization used for the dynamic programming) and demon-

strate performance improvements over a synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets: URLs and

EMBER. We also show that the performance of the learned Bloom filter improves with an increas-

ing number of partitions and that, in practice, a small number of regions (≈4 −6) suffices to get

a very good performance. We refer to our approach as the Partitioned Learned Bloom filter (PLBF).

Experimental results from both simulated and real-world datasets show significant performance im-

provements. We show that to achieve a false positive rate of 0.001, sandwiching uses 8.8x, 3.3x, and

1.2x the amount of space, and the AdaBF uses 6x, 2.5x, and 1.1x the amount of space compared to

PLBF for synthetic, URLs, and EMBER respectively.

*space saved by using our approach instead of a Bloom filter

2.1.1 Standard Bloom Filters and Related Variants

A standard Bloom filter, as described in Bloom’s original paper20, is for a set S = {x1, x2, ..., xn} of

n keys. It consists of an array of m bits and uses k independent hash functions {h1, h2, ...hk} with

the range of each hi being integer values between 0 and m −1. We assume that the hash functions

are fully random. Initially, all m bits are 0. For every key x ∈S, the array bits hi(x) are set to 1 for all

i ∈{1, 2, ...k}.

A membership query for y returns y ∈S if hi(y) = 1 for all i ∈{1, 2, ...k} and y ̸∈S otherwise.

This ensures that the Bloom filter does not have false negatives, but non-keys y might result in a false

Bloom filter design that achieves this lower bound for space, but it appears too complicated to use in

practice.

2.1.2 Learned Bloom Filter

Learned Bloom filters use learned models to beat the theoretical space bounds. Given a learned

model that can distinguish between keys and non-keys, learned Bloom filters use it as a pre-filter

before using backup Bloom filters. The backup Bloom filters can be any variant, including the stan-

dard, cuckoo, XOR filters, etc. If the model size is sufficiently small, learned models can enhance the

performance of any Bloom filter variant.

We provide a framework for learned Bloom filters. We are given a set of keys S = {x1, x2, .., xn}

from a universe U from which to build a Bloom filter. We are also given a sample of the non-keys Q,

representing the set U−S. Features that can help determine if an element is a member of S are deter-

mined. The learned model is then trained on the features of set S ∪Q for a binary classification task

and produces a score s(x) ∈[0, 1]. This score s(x) can be viewed (intuitively, not formally) as the

10


<!-- Page 21 -->


model’s confidence that the element x is in the set S. So, a key in S would ideally have a higher score

value than the non-keys. An assumption in this framework is that the training sample distribution

needs to match or be close to the test distribution of non-keys; the importance of this assumption

has been discussed at length by Mitzenmacher86. Past workloads or historical data can be used for

many applications to get an appropriate non-key sample.

As discussed above, Kraska et al.70 set a threshold t, and inputs satisfying s(x) > t are classified as

a key. A backup Bloom filter is built for the keys in S satisfying s(x) ≤t. This design is represented

in Figure 2.1A. Mitzenmacher86 proposes using another Bloom filter before the learned model and

a backup Bloom Filter. As the learned model is used between two Bloom filters as shown in Figure

2.1B, this is referred to as the ’sandwiching’ approach. They also analyze the optimal false-positive

rates for a given amount of memory for the two Bloom filters (given the false negative rate and false

positive rate for the learned model and the corresponding threshold). Interestingly, the sandwiching

approach and analysis can be seen as a special case of our approach and analysis, as described later

in Appendix A.4.1. Dai and Shrivastava33 use multiple thresholds to partition the score space into

numerous regions and use a backup Bloom filter for each score region. They propose heuristics for

dividing the score range and choosing a false-positive rate per region.

2.2 Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter (PLBF)

2.2.1 Design

As discussed, the general design segments the score space into multiple regions using multiple

thresholds, as shown in Figure 2.1C, and uses separate backup Bloom filters for each region. We

can choose different target false-positive rates for each region†. The parameters associated with each

†The different false-positive rates per region can be achieved in multiple ways. Either by choosing a separate Bloom filter per region or having a shared Bloom filter with a varying number of hash functions per region.

11

region are its threshold boundaries and its false positive rate. Setting good values for these parame-

ters is crucial for performance. We aim to analyze the performance of the learned Bloom filter with

respect to these parameters and find methods to determine optimal or near-optimal parameters.

The following notation will be important for our analysis. Let G(t) be the fraction of keys with

scores falling below t. Since the key set is finite, G(t) goes through discrete jumps. But it is helpful

(particularly in our pictures) to think of G(t) as being a continuous function, corresponding to a

cumulative probability distribution, with a corresponding “density” function g(t). For non-keys,

we assume that queries involving non-keys come from some distribution D, and we define H(t) to

be the probability that a non-key query from D has a score less than or equal to t. Note that non-key

query distribution might be different from the non-key distribution. If non-key queries are cho-

sen uniformly at random, then the non-key query distribution would be the same as the non-key

distribution. The theoretical analysis below assumes that H(t) is known. In practice, we expect a

good approximation of H(t) will be used, determined by taking samples from D or a suitably good

approximation, which may be based on, for example, historical data (discussed in detail by Mizen-

macher86). Here, H(t) can be viewed as a cumulative distribution function, and again, in our pic-

tures, we think of it as having a density h(t). Also, note that if queries for non-keys are chosen uni-

formly at random, then H(t) is just the fraction of non-keys with scores below t. While our analysis

holds generally, the example of H(t) being the fraction of non-keys with scores below t may be easier

to conceptualize. Visualization of the original learned Bloom filter in terms of these distributions is

shown in Figure 2.1D.

As we describe further below, for our partitioned learned Bloom filter, we use multiple thresh-

olds and a separate backup Bloom filter for each region, as shown in Figure 2.1E. In what follows,

we formulate the problem of choosing thresholds and backup Bloom filter false-positive rates (or

equivalently, sizes) as an optimization problem in Section 2.2.2. In Section 2.2.3, we find the opti-

mal solution of a relaxed problem, which helps us gain some insight into the general problem. We

then propose an approximate solution for the general problem in Section 2.2.3.

In our formulation, we find that the resulting parameters correspond to quite natural quantities

in terms of G and H. Specifically, a region’s optimal false positive rate is proportional to the ratio of

the fraction of keys to the fraction of non-keys in that region. Considering these region-based frac-

tions for keys and non-keys as probability distributions, the maximum space saving obtained is pro-

portional to the KL divergence between these distributions. Hence, we can optimize the thresholds

by choosing them to maximize this divergence. We can find thresholds to maximize this divergence

approximately through dynamic programming. We also show that this KL divergence increases with

more regions, and so does the performance. In our experiments, we find a small number(≈4 −6)

of partitions suffices to get good performance.

### 2.4 Conclusion

Our analysis of the partitioned learned Bloom filter provides a formal framework for improving

learned Bloom filter performance, which is substantially better than previous heuristics. However,

there are also limits to using a learned model in this fashion due to their costs. The model must first

be trained on the dataset and then must be retrained if the data is updated. Each query also requires

inference from the model in addition to the typical hashing operations. The compute and energy

requirements of training and inference for such models can, therefore, reduce the utility of a Bloom

filter depending on the use case. Despite this, the reduced memory footprint this technique can

achieve for structured data sets can still be compelling.

## Navigating Design-Space Tradeoffs:

## Proteus — A Self-Designing Range Filter

The Importance of Range Filters: Range queries are a fundamental operation in big data ap-

plications. Given a set S, a range query [a,b] returns the members of S within the query interval,

i.e. S ∩[a,b]. Example applications that need range queries and handle large amounts of data

include social media platforms using spatio-temporal queries to aggregate user events9, pattern

23


<!-- Page 34 -->


discovery and anomaly detection in time-series data streams69, scientific spatial models115, graph

databases38,72, and Blockchain analytics112. Range queries over such data sets are expensive due

to the disk or network costs required to process the data. Using a filter data structure to determine

when no elements are in the query range can improve performance by preventing unnecessary IO

operations.

As an important unifying application, large-scale data systems store large volumes of data on

cheap but high-latency storage devices. Answering range queries requires checking every data page

intersecting with the queried range to retrieve the relevant data. For example, in widely used Log-

Structured Merge (LSM) tree-based key-value stores, one or more pages must be checked per level8,29,43,73,104.

However, explicitly reading all intersecting data pages would be far too expensive. In this setting, a

compact range query data structure can be set up per page. Range query structures then act as fil-

ters, determining that no data in a range exists on a page (that is, we have an empty query) before

resorting to accessing storage. As such, much of our evaluation considers the effectiveness of range

filters in LSM trees.

Strong Guarantees are Impractical: Most work on filtering has been focused on single key queries.

Such filters are referred to as Approximate Membership Query structures (AMQs). AMQs such as

Bloom filters20 and their many variants are used to avoid the majority of unnecessary lookups for in-

dividual items in diverse applications. AMQs tolerate a small probability of false positives to achieve

a compact representation of the key set that supports membership queries. The false positive rate

(FPR) is the primary metric of a filter’s performance, as false positives incur unnecessary lookups

to verify their emptiness. Similar techniques can be applied to the approximate range emptiness

problem to avoid unnecessary range lookups, but guaranteeing a low FPR for all potential queries

can be expensive. Prior work has shown that to guarantee an FPR ε for range emptiness queries of

range size R requires Ω (log2(R) + log2(1/ε)) bits per key (BPK)51. Achieving a small FPR for all

queries, including for large ranges, therefore requires an undesirable memory budget.

Design Tradeoffs are Necessary For Performance: Current range filters aim to use less mem-

ory than theoretical worst-case guarantees require by not providing false positive guarantees for all

queries. Instead, state-of-the-art solutions prioritize particular types of workloads, such as those

with large ranges or queries that are correlated to the key set, by making hard-coded design deci-

depends on the relationship between the key and query sets, and provable guarantees are weak or

restricted to specific situations. These decisions limit their usefulness as deviation from the intended

with different data based on language, such as Wikipedia, exhibit temporal skew in query distribu-

requires the ability to prioritize the desired use case by navigating the range filter design space. How-

A Formal Framework Allows for Informed Designs: The standard metric for FPR analysis is

worst-case performance, which fails to capture the nuances of range filter design choices because

they are optimized for specific use cases. We introduce the Contextual Prefix FPR (CPFPR) model,

which formalizes how FPR varies across the design space of prefix-based filters. We focus on the

their design tradeoffs.

3.1 The Range Filter Design Space

Current solutions to the approximate range emptiness problem, or Approximate Range Emptiness

structures (AREs), use one of two fundamental design elements: probabilistic Approximate Mem-

bership Query data structures (AMQs) and deterministic search trees. Both strategies use prefixes of

the key set to encode the key space at different granularities.

AMQs are natural building blocks. They are designed to reduce unnecessary lookups by using

a compact representation of the data set that is small enough to fit in memory and supports fast

27


<!-- Page 38 -->


membership queries. For the representation to be sufficiently compact, a low non-zero false-positive

probability is tolerated but never a false negative. The search tree approach is more novel and explic-

itly encodes prefixes of the key set as a trie.

3.1.1 Probabilistic Prefix Filters

One method currently used by AREs is to include one or more AMQs that encode regions of the

key space with a single hashed value. There are many examples of AMQs, such as Bloom Filters20,

Cuckoo Filters45, Quotient Filters18, Xor Filters53, and Ribbon Filters41, which we will collectively

refer to as Bloom filters. Though their specifics vary, Bloom filters generally use one or more hash

functions to encode the key set as a compact array. Hashing allows for fast individual item lookups

with a low probability of false positives; however, valuable ordering information is lost in the hash-

ing process. To know whether a range [l, r] contains members of the key set, every key from l to

r would need to be queried individually, and the probability that at least one of them results in a

false positive is then proportional to r −l. As such, the usefulness of Bloom filters for such queries

rapidly declines with the size of the range being queried.

This can be compensated for by hashing unique prefixes of the key set rather than each key.

Hashing a given prefix encodes that there is at least one member of the key set with the given pre-

fix. This retains the benefits of hashing while allowing queries to the Bloom filter to rule out entire

regions of the key space at a time.

Prefix Bloom Filters: Prefix Bloom filters have been in use for some time now, particularly in the

context of network routing39. By hashing a key prefix of length l bits, the prefix Bloom filter en-

codes a region of the key space of size 2k−l, where k is the maximum key length. Using this strategy,

a range of the key space can be queried by querying the Bloom filter for each region that overlaps

with the desired range. This is well suited to situations with clustered target ranges, like IP addresses

in network routing, as the prefix length used can be tuned to the cluster sizes. Prefix Bloom filters

28


<!-- Page 39 -->


are also used in key-value stores, but the constraint of encoding the key space as fixed size, prefix-

defined regions limits their usefulness when the target ranges are not well known. In particular,

prefix Bloom filters are susceptible to the choice of prefix length, which we discuss in more detail in

Section 3.2.

Rosetta: Rosetta79 is an ARE aimed specifically at range queries in database systems using LSM

trees, such as RocksDB60. These systems have used prefix Bloom filters with shorter prefixes to filter

out large-range queries; however, if they are not correctly tuned, these prefix filters perform very

poorly on small to medium-range queries and individual key queries. This becomes even worse if

the queries are correlated to the key set, and empty queries tend to fall close to the key set.

Conceptually, Rosetta encodes the nodes of an implicit segment tree, or binary trie, representing

the entire key space. All nodes of a given depth present in the key set are encoded by hashing the

corresponding prefixes into a single Bloom filter. The prefix filter encoding the tree’s leaf nodes is

equivalent to a Bloom filter populated with full key hashes. A range is queried by checking for the

presence of each node in the sub-tree corresponding to that range in depth-first order. If any node is

not present in its respective prefix filter, the entire sub-tree rooted at that node is known to be empty

and is not queried further. If a given node may be present, the sub-tree continues to be queried in

depth-first order until either a leaf node is reported as present, resulting in a positive range query, or

the entire sub-tree is found to be empty.

In practice, Rosetta does not encode every level of this tree and is configured by apportioning the

total memory budget between the prefix Bloom filters encoding each prefix length. In particular,

Rosetta typically allocates its memory budget to the last few prefix lengths. This allocation strategy

works well for small ranges and point queries, regardless of proximity to the key set; however, larger

range queries will still require many Bloom filter queries to cover the query range and performance

trends towards that of an AMQ.

29


<!-- Page 40 -->


3.1.2 Deterministic Prefix Filters

Other solutions forgo the benefits of hashing to retain as much ordering information as possible.

These AREs typically use an explicitly encoded search tree, which performs a similar role to the

implicit tree encoded by Rosetta. In particular, tries are a well-studied method of encoding prefixes

in a succinct search tree14,19,46. To fit these trees in memory, they must be pruned down to the key

set’s prefixes. As before, each prefix in the tree represents a range with at least one member of the key

set, while any prefix not found in the tree will not be present in the key set. The pruning, therefore,

introduces the possibility of false positives due to common prefixes between keys and non-keys.

These trees are more flexible than prefix Bloom filters in certain aspects. They can easily encode

prefixes of different lengths within the same structure, and all sub-prefixes are also retained. This

comes with the downside of paying more memory for longer prefixes since the entire prefix must

be explicitly stored, as opposed to prefix Bloom filters, which can dedicate available memory to any

individual prefix length.

SuRF: The Succinct Range Filter (SuRF)116 is a state-of-the-art ARE that encodes prefixes of the

key set as a Fast Succinct Trie (FST). It is a static filter and does not adapt to queries. The FST in

SuRF combines the sparse and dense Level-Order Unary Degree Sequence (LOUDS) representa-

tions from Jacobson64 to achieve an efficient trie encoding (LOUDS-DS), which allows SuRF to

encode longer prefixes than other trie-based prefix filters on the same memory budget. This encod-

ing can also be searched in constant time, so the query time is independent of the size of the range.

Despite this, encoding every full key in the FST is typically too expensive, so SuRF’s base configura-

tion prunes the branch for each key to the minimum length prefix that uniquely identifies it in the

key set. If additional memory is available, it can be used to extend these prefixes. It can also be used

to store hashes of the key suffixes to help rule out individual keys, though these do not provide any

long enough to be uniquely identified in the key set also means that the distribution of the keys

issue in situations where tight memory budgets must be strictly maintained.

3.2.2 Tractable Tries

By using two Bloom filters with different prefix lengths, one can reasonably address divergent query

workloads, but their probabilistic nature can still pose issues. As discussed before, the longer prefix

length is not well suited for large ranges, and any l1 prefix entirely within Q that results in a false

positive will require 2l2−l1 prefix queries at l2. If there is much difference between l1 and l2, which is

likely if two Bloom filters are justified, then the second Bloom filter will have a very low probability

of catching more extensive ranges missed by the first. We could reduce the number of false positives

at the first Bloom filter by allocating a more significant proportion of the memory; however, this

also reduces the filter’s ability to deal with correlated queries since this memory must be taken from

the second Bloom filter.

3.3.1 Hybrid Architecture

Unlike the other filters we have discussed, Proteus uses probabilistic and deterministic encodings of

the key space: an FST and a prefix Bloom filter. Unlike SuRF, the FST in Proteus does not encode

a unique prefix for every key, but rather all unique key prefixes of a fixed length, resulting in a FST

with uniform depth. Recall that SuRF prunes the branch for each key to the minimum length pre-

fix that uniquely identifies it in the key set and can extend these prefixes with explicitly stored key

37


<!-- Page 48 -->


bits. Similarly, in the Proteus FST, any trie branch encoding a single key is extended to the chosen

trie depth by explicitly storing the additional key bits rather than using the LOUDS-DS trie encod-

ing. A toy example of a Proteus encoding a 24-bit key space is shown in Figure 3.3 using a trie depth

and Bloom filter prefix length of 16 and 20 bits, respectively.

A uniform trie depth is used in part because it simplifies the modeling process and also because

we believe it is a better use of memory. The intuition here is that sparse regions of the key space that

use a coarse encoding are highly susceptible to false positives since they encode very large empty sub-

regions. Similarly, encoding a densely populated portion of the key space at a coarse granularity will

only result in small empty subregions that are less likely to cause false positives. SuRF requires a

unique prefix for each key to support queries other than range emptiness, such as range counts and

sums; however, this also imposes a minimal memory requirement and limits its usefulness for situ-

ations with strict memory constraints. Alternatively, a uniform depth can be adjusted to fit within

any memory constraint, and any leftover memory can still be used in the Bloom filter. While Pro-

teus does not support range queries other than emptiness queries, replacing the Bloom filter with

a counting Bloom filter would provide this functionality22. The Bloom filter is assigned a prefix

length between the maximum key length and the depth of the trie.

Proteus reaps the benefits of both encodings while also mitigating their shortcomings. The trie

efficiently rules out large ranges in constant time, while the prefix Bloom filter can be positioned to

catch most of the queries that would fall within the empty sub-regions encoded by the trie. Careful

choice of the Bloom filter’s prefix length will also improve the prefix Bloom filter’s performance in-

dependent of the trie. When exploring the configuration space, Proteus is free to dedicate its entire

memory budget to either encoding, so it can be entirely probabilistic or deterministic, depending

on the context. Configuring Proteus amounts to choosing the prefix lengths for the trie and Bloom

filter. The memory budget limits the possible prefix lengths of the trie, while any memory not used

in the trie can be assigned to any single prefix length using the Bloom filter.

3.3.2 Operations

Queries in Proteus are carried out by searching the combined structure for any members of Ql2 in

depth-first order. If any prefix x ∈Ql1 ∩Kl1 is found in the trie, then the prefixes y ∩Ql2 s.t. x is

or return a false positive, the query ends and returns positive. If all prefixes return negative at the

Bloom filter, the query continues to the next matching leaf node in the trie. If no more valid leaves

are in the trie and all queried Bloom filter regions have returned negative, the query returns negative.

Queries that land sufficiently far from the key set are then ruled out in the trie as lcp(Q, K) will be

short, while queries that land closer to the key set must rely on the Bloom filter. In Figure 3.3, the

∅, so the query will return negative so long as none of the prefixes queried at the Bloom filter result

in false positives.

3.5 System Evaluation: RocksDB

We integrate Proteus into RocksDB —a popular key-value store —and demonstrate that it improves

end-to-end range query performance by up to 3.9x and 3.3x over Rosetta and SuRF, respectively,

across a variety of workloads, with consistently better performance at low BPKs (8-12). This speed-

up is due to reduced I/O operations resulting from the lower FPR achieved. Furthermore, we show

51


<!-- Page 62 -->


that the additional cost of modeling in filter construction does not significantly impact the end-

to-end performance of RocksDB and that Proteus can adapt smoothly to changes in the query

workload distribution, unlike Rosetta and SuRF, which suffer drastic declines in performance on

certain adversarial distributions. The experiments here use integer keys; see Appendix B for a similar

evaluation using string keys.

3.5.1 Proteus System Integration

RocksDB uses an LSM tree architecture that organizes data on disk into levels of increasing size,

where each level Li (except L0) is range partitioned into multiple sorted runs or Static Sorted Ta-

ble (SST) files that occupy disjoint key ranges. The SST files in L0 are directly flushed to disk from

MemTables —in-memory structures that buffer writes —and thus typically have overlapping key

ranges. Static filters (e.g., Bloom filters) are built for every SST file to reduce unnecessary accesses for

non-existent keys. When a level Li reaches its maximum capacity, RocksDB selectively merges SST

files from Li into Li+1, triggering the construction of new filters on the merged data in the new Li+1

SST files. This process is called compaction.

Range Query Implementation: Similar to79, we modify the RocksDB closed Seek logic to first

check all filters for the existence of keys in the queried range. If all filters return false, then Seek re-

turns an invalid iterator. For the filters that return true, RocksDB retrieves the lowest keys from the

associated SST files that are greater than or equal to the lower query bound. This is done by binary

searching over the index blocks, which store min/max information in each SST file, and fetching the

corresponding data block. If the global smallest key is smaller than the upper query bound, an iter-

ator pointing to that key is returned. Otherwise, an invalid iterator is returned for the empty range

query.

Sample Query Queue: Since Proteus (and Rosetta) need sample queries, we create a fixed-size

query queue and seed it with an initial query sample. Older queries are evicted with a FIFO policy.

52


<!-- Page 63 -->


This changing set of sample queries is used with the keys in each SST file to determine the optimal

filter design for each SST file at construction time. In our experiments, we use a queue size of 20K

queries (~320KB) and update the queue with every 100th executed empty query.

*Figure 3.6: Proteus improves end-to-end RocksDB performance on low memory budgets across diverse workloads.*

Tuning RocksDB: Since all filters have to be queried during a closed Seek, we curtail this CPU

cost by tuning RocksDB to fit more data in each SST file, thereby reducing the number of filters

queried. This also helps to control the overall cost of modeling from filter construction when there

are heavy compactions. We increase the SST file size from the default of 64MB to 256MB and scale

up the size of L1 and the MemTables to maintain the same number of SST files that fit in them with

default settings.‡ Similarly, we selectively enable data compression for specific levels. We leave the

few SST files in L0 and L1 uncompressed to maintain the speed of MemTable flushes and L0 →L1

compactions. For SST files in L2, we use LZ4 compression —a light-weight compression algorithm

recommended by RocksDB63 that balances CPU cost and compression size. We use heavy-weight

ZSTD compression for SST files in L3 onwards as they are less frequently modified and contain the

bulk of the data in the LSM tree. We ensure that the filters are cached in the RocksDB block cache§

and assign RocksDB 6 background threads for flushes and compactions.

3.5.3 End-to-End Performance

We measure the end-to-end range query performance regarding workload execution latency for Pro-

teus, SuRF, and Rosetta on four use cases targeting different points in the design space. As shown

in Figure 3.6, Proteus achieves the lowest latency across all workloads on low memory budgets, im-

proving upon SuRF and Rosetta by as much as 3.3x and 3.9x, respectively. In RocksDB, one of

the primary sources of latency is I/O when accessing the SST files. A lower FPR generally results

in lower latency because we can avoid unnecessary I/O. However, thrashing in RocksDB’s inter-

nal cache or excessive prefix queries during Bloom filter probes can result in higher latency despite

a low FPR. For example, Rosetta improves its FPR on Normal-Uniform as its memory budget

increases by using more hash functions per Bloom filter, but the resulting latency increases. This

is because a large-range query requires Rosetta to query many prefixes, and the CPU cost for each

is proportional to the number of hash functions used. Proteus can frequently avoid this as the trie

limits - and sometimes eliminates all - prefix queries made at the Bloom filter. SuRF’s computa-

tional cost for queries is effectively constant, but it can suffer due to pressure on RockDB’s internal

cache. This can be seen in both the Normal-Split and Uniform-Correlated workloads. We

observed that SuRF puts more pressure on RocksDB’s internal cache, which results in thrashing

### 3.6 Related Work

Our investigation is part of a broader system community initiative to design contextually cus-

tomized data structures.

Adaptive Range Filter: The Adaptive Range Filter (ARF)7 adapts its binary trie structure in re-

sponse to queries, extending branches to compensate for false positives and retracting them to

57


<!-- Page 68 -->


maintain its memory footprint. However, ARF’s encoding strategy limits memory efficiency and

requires significant time and memory to pre-train116. Similar adaptive techniques have been applied

to AMQs to deal with adversarial workloads88,17.

Stacked Filters: Stacked Filters37 also use modeling to incorporate workload-specific information

in their design. However, their model is designed for point rather than range queries.

Data Calculator: Similar to PRFs, the Data Calculator59 breaks down a complex design space into

its fundamental design primitives and models the behavior of designs to determine the optimal de-

sign for a given workload. However, the Data Calculator focuses on the design space of key-value

structures rather than range filters and merely synthesizes the optimal design rather than instantiat-

ing it.

Learned Structures: Several iterations of learned Bloom filters use learned models to leverage pat-

terns in the data for better performance87,108,33. These filters are designed for single-item queries

and perform poorly on range queries for the same reasons as other AMQs. This method of fitting to

the use case also requires the presence of patterns in the data that are amenable to the model being

used. Similar techniques have been applied to indexing database structures to speed up searches70.

Indexes can also be used to answer range queries, but they are larger, general-purpose structures that

typically require more I/O to answer a query.

3.7 Summary and Opportunities

This chapter introduces Proteus, a self-designing range filter with robust performance across var-

ious workloads. The core idea is that (1) Proteus unifies the design spaces of state-of-the-art range

filters to cover a wider range of workloads and (2) can instantiate workload-optimal designs. Ana-

lyzing cutting-edge range filtering techniques through the lens of the CPFPR model reveals adver-

sarial workloads that no current design can handle practically, suggesting the need to expand the

58


<!-- Page 69 -->


range filter design space further. Other promising directions include extending the CPFPR model

to support higher-order optimization strategies by incorporating metrics such as query latency and

exploring non-uniform memory allocation strategies in RocksDB.

## 4

## Navigating Design-Space Tradeoffs:

## Multi-Queue SSD Latency Modeling

Understanding the performance of storage devices and the implications for data structure design

is non-trivial due to factors such as seek times, caching, scheduling, parallelism, flash wear-out, and

garbage collection. For this reason, researchers and designers have long used analytical frameworks

such as the Disk Access Machine (DAM), Parallel Disk Access Machine (PDAM), and Affine mod-

60


<!-- Page 71 -->


els, which provide a simplified view of I/O performance but capture enough performance-critical

features to evaluate the relative performance of different structures and design choices6,99. For ex-

ample, the DAM model only considers the number of pages that must be transferred from main

memory to storage and vice versa; however, this was sufficient to explain the benefits of B-trees and

their rise to prominence in the 70s32 as well as the more recent prevalence of write-optimized struc-

tures such as Be-trees and Log-Structured Merge-trees (LSM-trees)65,94. The PDAM and Affine

models are both fairly simple refinements of the DAM model, which consider parallelism and seek

time, respectively. These minor refinements have led to more accurate predictions for different types

of storage hardware, such as Hard Disk Drives (HDDs) and Solid State Drives (SSDs), and have

provided greater insight into design choices such as node size in B-trees vs. Be-trees16.

However, advances in storage technology have outpaced our abstractions for I/O, leading to sub-

stantial gaps in the insight they can provide. For example, the move from mechanical addressing in

HDDs to electrical addressing and out-of-place updates in SSDs has significantly reduced overall

latency; however, it has also introduced several overheads related to writes and garbage collection to

manage flash wear-out resulting in asymmetric read and write performance105. The address transla-

tions required for out-of-place updates also have significant implications for performance. The or-

der in which pages are accessed directly impacts the efficiency of the devices’ Flash Translation Layer

(FTL)105. Modern multi-queue SSDs are also designed to use Peripheral Component Intercon-

nect Express (PCIe) and support much higher transfer speeds and overall throughput than previous

Serial AT Attachment (SATA) HDDs and SSDs1,4,81. However, the highly parallel architectures

of these devices require high levels of concurrent access to fully utilize their potential, as reflected

by their use of the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) protocol, which provides multiple I/O

queues directly accessible by applications3. The resulting performance profile for a multi-queue

SSD is then sensitive to several factors, including concurrency, order of access, and write intensity.

I/O models that do not consider these factors will naturally be less accurate and provide less insight

61


<!-- Page 72 -->


when evaluating storage algorithms.

To illustrate this, consider a basic file I/O benchmark designed to demonstrate the effects of con-

currency and order of access on latency and throughput. We use k threads to read k GB of data con-

currently from a 50 GB file, each thread reading 1 GB of data using r equally sized sequential reads

starting at staggered random offsets, resulting in r random accesses per thread. We then vary r from

0.1% to 100% of pages read and k from 1 to 128, resulting in rk random page reads for a given trial.

We use staggered random offsets to ensure that no two threads read the same data simultaneously.

Between the staggering and the file size, the vast majority of randomly accessed pages will result in

cache misses for the device.

The DAM model would suggest that the total latency of this experiment is purely dependent on

the total amount of I/O with no correlation to r and that throughput will be constant with respect

to k. Similarly, the PDAM model predicts no correlation with r but does account for an increase

in throughput proportional to the device’s hardware-level parallelism, i.e., the number of physical

channels to the device’s flash backend. By contrast, the Affine model can reasonably predict the ef-

fects of random access for a single thread but does not capture how this changes with the addition of

more threads. None of these models would predict any difference if we performed writes instead of

reads. In practice, we observe that single-threaded read performance varies by upwards of 10x with

respect to r across multiple devices and upwards of 26x for writes. Moreover, we see this relationship

change as we increase k and throughput that scales well beyond the level of hardware parallelism.

When we add to this substantially different performance profiles for writes vs reads, the limits of

these I/O models become rather glaring.

Despite this, the need for storage algorithms optimized for such hardware is only increasing.

Multi-queue SSDs have become increasingly prevalent, gaining widespread adoption in the cloud

and in enterprise deployments - not only are they cheap and fast, but recent advancements in the

NVMe-over-Fabric protocol have made disaggregated flash storage even more tractable31,55. How-

62


<!-- Page 73 -->


ever, existing database systems and storage engines are not designed to exploit the performance of

multi-queue SSDs fully56. Closing this gap will require new storage algorithms and paradigms,

which our current I/O abstractions are not equipped to assess.

In this paper, we present the Multi-Queue SSD (MQSSD) model, which can capture the im-

pacts of concurrency and random access on modern hardware with respect to both reads and writes.

We build off the knowledge of existing I/O models, as described in Section 4.1.1, and base our new

model on the performance critical characteristics of multi-queue SSDs described in Section 4.1.2.

In Section 4.2.1 we define the MQSSD model and in Section 4.2.2 we validate it and previous mod-

els against real hardware using the file I/O benchmark described earlier. The comparison of these

models described earlier can be seen in Figure 4.3 along with the MQSSD model. In Section 4.3,

we demonstrate how the MQSSD model can be used to evaluate and optimize a real-world storage

engine designed for flash storage, Facebook’s RocksDB, resulting in improvements of up to 4.38x

in write throughput over default settings while also achieving optimal query and scan performance.

In Section 4.4, we compare our work against other related projects. Finally, in Section 4.5, we con-

clude that the MQSSD model provides greater accuracy and insight than previous I/O models when

designing and optimizing storage systems for modern hardware.

### 4.1 Background

We now describe in detail the existing I/O models we build upon and aspects of multi-queue SSDs

we want our model to capture.

4.1.1 Current I/O Models

The DAM model, also called the external memory model or I/O model, introduced by Aggarwal

and Vitter in ’886, has been the primary model for I/O analysis for the last few decades. The core as-

63


<!-- Page 74 -->


sumptions of this model are that main memory and storage are primarily differentiated by their size,

access granularity, and access latency, which remains true of storage hardware to this day. Despite

this, relatively simple changes can substantially improve the model’s accuracy, as we will see with the

PDAM and affine models.

The DAM Model

The DAM model captures the fundamental relation between any two levels of the memory hier-

archy; however, we focus on the context of main memory and storage, for which the model was

initially intended. We have the following parameters:

N: The number of records/size of the working set. Each record is assumed to have a unit size.

M: The number of records that can fit in main memory.

B: The number of sequentially stored records that can be transferred to or from storage in a

single page, i.e., our granularity of access.

In this model, our latency unit is page transfers, i.e., reading a page into memory or writing it back to

storage, the idea being that the latency of a single page transfer is on a different order of magnitude

than in-memory computation. For example, modern Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM)

latency is on the order of nanoseconds vs. milliseconds for modern HDDs2,5. Due to their different

orders of magnitude in latency, in-memory computation is considered free in this context. It also

assumes that 1 ≤B ≤M < N.

The PDAM Model

The PDAM model is a variation of the DAM model also introduced by Aggarwal and Vitter in ’886

that was designed to represent HDDs with some level of concurrent access with multiple read/write

64


<!-- Page 75 -->


heads, e.g., RAID0. To account for this, the PDAM adds the following parameter to the DAM:

P: The number of pages that can be transferred concurrently.

Since this model allows for multiple transfers at a time at no additional cost, it no longer makes sense

to consider individual page transfers as our baseline latency unit. Instead, we consider the number of

I/O cycles during which up to P pages can be concurrently transferred. If we fix P = 1, this is then

equivalent to the DAM model. The PDAM model also assumes 1 ≤P ≤⌊M/B⌋. More recent

work by Bender et al. has shown that this model can reasonably predict SSD performance when P is

taken to be the number of physical channels to flash on the device in the context of concurrent-read-

exclusive-write I/O16.

The Affine Model

Introduced by Ruemmler and Wilkes in ’9499, the Affine model is a refinement of the DAM that

place. This is the only cost for sequentially accessed pages.

In this model, reading or writing N consecutive records to or from disk costs s + αN

SSDs use electrical addressing vs. the mechanical addressing this model is based on; however, for

4.1.2 Characteristics of Multi-Queue SSDs

All of the models we have discussed so far were designed to reflect the performance characteristics

of HDDs. However, as SSDs have become cheaper, larger, and longer lasting, they have increasingly

replaced HDDs in applications. Multi-queue SSDs using the NVMe protocol, in particular, have

delivered unprecedented performance regarding latency and throughput and are particularly ben-

eficial for I/O intensive applications113. We now describe the aspects of multi-queue SSDs that are

performance-critical for I/O-intensive applications. For additional details on the internals of mod-

ern, multi-queue SSDs, we recommend the work of Tavakkol et al.105.

Electrical Addressing & the FTL

One of the most significant recent changes in storage technology has been the move to electrical ad-

dressing. Rather than spinning platters with magnetic read/write heads, SSDs typically use NAND

flash, which can be read or written simply by passing current through a circuit. This drastically re-

duces the latency of storage access and fundamentally changes how storage devices operate. Unlike

with HDDs, flash pages must be physically erased before they can be overwritten, which requires the

use of out-of-place updates. Every time a page is updated, its contents are copied to a new page along

with the updates, and then the old page is marked for garbage collection. The logical address used by

an application is thus given a new physical address used by the storage device each time it is updated.

The Flash Translation Layer (FTL) records these address translations and updates on flash. Beyond

the mapping table, the FTL also manages the onboard DRAM cache, garbage collection, and flash

transaction scheduling. As we describe shortly, the latency of access to storage depends on how well

the FTL can use its available resources, namely the DRAM cache and multiple channels to flash,

which must also be used for garbage collection.

Asymmetric Reads & Writes

Before discussing the FTL’s bottlenecks, we consider the effects of electrical addressing on our basic

operations. Unlike HDDs, where reads and writes operate in the same way, out-of-place updates

make writes inherently more expensive than reads as they require additional transactions with flash.

For example, consider reading or writing a single page, temporarily ignoring the DRAM cache.

In either case, we must first translate the requested address from logical to physical, and then the

requested page must be read. In the case of a read, these two flash transactions will be sufficient:

one to read the mapping table and one to read the data. In the case of a write, we must also write

the updated data to a new page, mark the old physical address as invalid, and update the mapping

69


<!-- Page 80 -->


table with the new address. This requires up to three additional transactions with flash (write new,

invalidate old, update mapping) without even considering garbage collection. As we discuss in the

rest of this section, a number of other factors, such as garbage collection and caching, can either

exacerbate or mitigate this difference in cost, depending on the situation. As a result, the difference

in cost is not just a constant factor and must be considered more carefully.

Flash Wear-out & Garbage Collection

Despite the overheads, out-of-place updates are used to extend the lifespan of flash storage. Flash

cells have a limited lifespan due to wear caused by usage. While reads cause minor wear to the cells,

writing and (especially) erasing take a significant toll due to the amount of charge required95.

Therefore, it is necessary to evenly disperse writes across all physical pages and minimize the wear

caused by each erase cycle. Out-of-place updates facilitate the former as every write is always to an

arbitrary new physical page. The FTL can then send incoming logical writes to physical pages that

have been erased the fewest number of times, a process known as wear leveling 109. To extend the

number of erase cycles each page can withstand, pages are erased in contiguous groups called blocks,

reducing the total charge required for the operation95.

While this combination of techniques has been quite effective at extending the longevity of SSDs,

writing and erasing at two different granularities introduces complications. As an SSD is used, it will

eventually reach a steady state where the number of valid, invalid, and free pages stays pretty con-

sistent. Though the precise distribution of these depends on the workload and garbage collection

algorithm, most steady states have very few free flash blocks109. As a result, high write pressure can

make passively waiting to reclaim blocks when they are ready infeasible. In such cases, the device

must reclaim blocks by actively relocating valid pages until it can free up an entire block. This results

in high hardware write amplification, which we define as the ratio of data written to flash by the

device to data the host system requested written.

70


<!-- Page 81 -->


Caching for Sequential vs. Random Access

We must also consider the FTL’s DRAM cache and its performance implications for the access or-

der. Recall that the primary cause of latency in most I/O requests is performing transactions with

flash and that the mapping table itself is stored on flash. If the mapping is not cached when translat-

ing a given address, it must be read from flash. However, the mapping table is read a page at a time,

so Θ(B) logically sequential page mappings are read into or written back from the cache per flash

transaction with the mapping table. Consider if an application requests to read N records stored

sequentially. This results in a request for Θ(N

B ) pages, as each page is being made full use of, and the

FTL only needs to read Θ( N

B2 ) pages from the mapping table as it retrieves Θ(B) useful mappings

with each transaction. Conversely, if an application requests to read N records stored on different

pages at random logical addresses, not only will this result in a request for Θ(N) pages of records,

since each page only contains a single record of interest, but the FTL will also need to read Θ(N)

pages from the mapping table as each page is only guaranteed to have a single helpful mapping. Sim-

ilarly, for writes, the initial mapping translation and updates to the mapping table can be done in

batches of Θ(B) if the requested pages are logically sequential but will require additional flash trans-

actions per page written if the requested pages are logically random. The resulting relationship be-

tween sequential vs. random I/O is similar to that observed in HDDs but with different constants

for writes and reads due to their asymmetric costs.

High-throughput & Concurrent Access

A significant innovation in SSD architecture has been the introduction of high-bandwidth inter-

faces like the NVMe protocol, which is designed to take advantage of the parallel structure with

multiple physical channels to the flash back end, which itself has a highly hierarchical architecture

to facilitate I/O concurrency further3,105. Unlike the SATA protocol designed for HDDs, which

71


<!-- Page 82 -->


provides a single I/O port managed by the OS, the NVMe protocol provides multiple I/O queues

directly accessible by applications1. Bypassing the OS also allows the device driver to schedule I/O

requests based on the device’s available resources. Taking full advantage of these devices’ available

bandwidth naturally requires concurrent access from one or more applications. While there is some

amount of overhead at the FTL associated with having to schedule additional concurrent requests,

being able to take full advantage of all channels to flash more than makes up for it. Having more

concurrent accesses than the number of flash channels can also be beneficial as the FTL can more

fully saturate all of its internal I/O queues, except if there is too much write pressure, as discussed

previously.

4.3.1 LSM Trees & Compaction

Unlike a B-tree, LSM trees forgo global ordering and in-place updates to support faster ingestion;

instead, data is partitioned temporally into levels of exponentially increasing size. Incoming key-

value pairs are first buffered in memory and then flushed to storage as sorted immutable runs, which

are later sort-merged using sequential I/O. Runs are first flushed to the smallest level, L0, and as data

accumulates in a given level, it will eventually be sort-merged into the next level92. This sort-merge

operation, referred to as compaction, is fundamental to an LSM-tree’s performance as it reduces

read and space amplification at the cost of write amplification† 60,78,101. Additional strategies are

used to reduce I/O and improve read performance, including auxiliary indexing and membership

structures like fence pointers, tries, and probabilistic filters34,60,68,116. For this demonstration, we

focus on the I/O performance implications of different compaction strategies when backed by a

multi-queue SSD. Sarkar et al. present the compaction design space as an ensemble of 4 primitives:

(i) the trigger or when we decide to compact two or more runs, (ii) the data layout or how the

data is organized, (iii) the granularity or how much data is compacted at once, and (iv) the data

movement policy or which data should be compacted101. We recommend their work for a more

detailed description of the compaction design space, including an online compaction dictionary,

Compactionary100, with helpful visualizations. Of particular interest to us will be the data layout,

which generally comprises some combination of tiering and/or leveling 34,78,101. Below, we describe

in more detail how RocksDB implements each primitive and explain tiering and leveling in that

context.

†In this section, write amplification refers to data structure write amplification as defined in Section 4.1.1. Read and space amplification are defined analogously.

Compaction in RocksDB

RocksDB’s standard data layout combines tiering and leveling. The first level, L0, is tiered, and

all subsequent levels use leveling. All sorted runs are partitioned by key range into Static Sorted

Table (SST) files roughly the same size. Tiering for L0 means that files are not merged together,

but each acts as a separate sorted run with potentially overlapping key ranges. As with tiering in

general, this reduces write amplification at L0 as no data is ever rewritten within the level but incurs

higher read amplification since every file in the level must be checked when retrieving a given key-

value pair. By contrast, leveling maintains a single sorted run per level, which results in lower read

amplification at the cost of higher write amplification since we perform a sort-merge every time

more data is added to the level35,78,94,101. The standard compaction trigger occurs when a given

level exceeds its capacity, as determined by the capacity growth factor between levels. The size of

L0 is controlled independently. The RocksDB documentation suggests making L0 and L1 similar

in size, which is how we have configured our benchmarks60. Once compaction is triggered at Li,

the data movement policy picks the file in Li that overlaps with the fewest files in Li+1 to minimize

write amplification. If required, multiple files can be chosen to return Li to its target size. Multiple

compactions at Li can be performed in parallel, assuming they do not touch the same files in Li+1.

In the case of L0, since most files have overlapping key ranges, there is little opportunity for parallel

compaction; however, specifically for compaction from L0 to L1, RocksDB allows for subcompacts

that partition individual compactions by key range into multiple concurrent operations.

Consider a data set, S, consisting of N bytes of key-value pairs with a uniform distribution of keys.

We want to compare the cost of inserts, updates, deletes, queries, and scans for an LSM tree built

on S using RocksDB’s implementation across various tuning parameters. In an LSM tree, inserts,

removed entirely if the most recent value is a delete message. Our measure of performance for these

operations is the latency of compaction operations. For a query, we consider the latency of retriev-

Insights

As with the DAM model, our analysis of leveled compaction in RocksDB gives us the standard

tradeoff between read and write performance with respect to F. A larger fanout results in more write

amplification due to more aggressive merging and less read amplification since there are fewer to-

tal sorted runs. As with the Affine model, we see a similar tradeoff between write amplification and

83


<!-- Page 94 -->


scan performance with respect to T. Larger files mean we must rewrite more data during each com-

paction, but they also result in larger amounts of sequential data and, therefore, fewer random ac-

cesses when performing scans over large amounts of data. This tradeoff is slightly more nuanced,

though, as larger files do not increase random accesses for compression, only the amount of data

being transferred at bandwidth cost. RocksDB already strikes a good balance with respect to these

tradeoffs using a fanout of 10 and 64 MB files by default.

More importantly than fanout or file size, we also see that all of our read and write costs depend

on the level of concurrency we can leverage. As shown in our micro benchmarks in Section 4.2.2,

the level of concurrency can change these costs by as much as 19x, which can be much greater than

the impact of fanout or file size, as we will see in the following section. However, the data struc-

ture’s ability to facilitate concurrent access is an important consideration. RocksDB can leverage

as much read concurrency as the user provides58,60 using out-of-place updates and asynchronous

reads. RocksDB does not currently provide any options for leveraging additional query or scan

concurrency under the hood. RocksDB does offer more options concerning compactions. As men-

tioned, multiple compactions can occur at different levels or within the same level if they do not

touch the same files. We can then control the maximum concurrency level by the compaction thread

pool size. By default, RocksDB only allocates a single background thread for compaction.

RocksDB’s standard layout limits the amount of concurrency that can be leveraged since concur-

rent compactions cannot touch the same files. This also has implications for file size, as larger files

would further reduce the opportunities for concurrent compactions. We propose a somewhat un-

orthodox layout: a single level to leverage concurrency and large files without changing RocksDB’s

implementation. This takes the idea of leveling to its logical extreme; we maintain a single sorted

run by aggressively merging all incoming data into L1. Under conventional wisdom, this provides

optimal performance for queries and scans (assuming fixed file size) as there is only a single sorted

run, which comes at the cost of very high write amplification. While this remains true in our model,

84


<!-- Page 95 -->


we can completely offset the cost of write amplification with high concurrency. In particular, we can

leverage RocksDB’s subcompactions, which are limited to compaction into L1, for all compaction

operations.

### 4.4 Related Work

Other recent work has been related to modeling the performance of multi-queue SSDs, but it

has primarily focused on emulation and simulation. Projects such as SimpleSSD66, Amber52,

MQSim105, and MQSim-E75 model the SSD in fine-grained detail at the architectural level. These

simulators incorporate many individual models representing the state of the various components

within the SSD. While these are immensely helpful for exploring the effects of architectural design

choices, they are not ideal for software design, as running a full simulation to test a design can be

quite computationally expensive and time-consuming. Furthermore, they provide a level of detail

that can be opaque to those not intimately familiar with SSD architectures.

Other projects like Cosmos+71 and FEMU77 have taken the route of emulation, which aims to

fully replicate the operations of the SSD using either software or a configurable hardware platform.

Even without the hardware platforms being prohibitively expensive, such emulators are intended as

drop-in replacements for the SSD and require implementing and running software to gain any sort

of insights.

In contrast with both of these goals, we do not aim to achieve this level of fidelity in our analysis.

Rather, we aim to provide a framework for informative comparisons at the earlier stages of software

development that lends itself to formal reasoning (proofs) as well as lightweight approximations for

online optimization.

### 4.5 Conclusion

In this chapter, we present the MQSSD model, a storage abstraction for algorithmic analysis based

on modern multi-queue SSDs. We review and demonstrate the hardware characteristics the MQSSD

model is designed to capture, while also demonstrating how previous I/O abstractions fail to do so.

We apply our model to Facebook’s LSM-tree-based key-value store, RocksDB, and demonstrate that

91


<!-- Page 102 -->


optimizing for modern storage hardware may require a shift in our thinking about I/O. In partic-

ular, we show that a configuration that previously would have been considered unorthodox actu-

ally improves throughput for all operations by better-utilizing concurrency. We conclude that the

MQSSD model provides a more accurate abstraction of modern hardware than previous models,

allowing for a greater degree of insight and optimization.

## 5

## Conclusion

This dissertation describes multiple methods of applying computational models to data struc-

ture and algorithm design for systems. Chapter 2 introduces the Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter

(PLBF), which provides a formal framework for improving the performance of machine-learning-

enhanced Bloom filters. Chapter 3 describes Proteus, a self-designing range filter that utilizes the

Contextual Prefix False-Positive Rate (CPFPR) model to navigate the range-filter design space and

achieve robust performance across various workloads. Chapter 4 presents the Multi-Queue Solid

93


<!-- Page 104 -->


State Drive (MQSSD) model, a new storage abstraction for algorithmic analysis based on mod-

ern storage hardware. Each of these use cases leverages computational models to achieve context-

informed designs.

The key principle across these methods is formalizing the relationship between software design,

hardware, and the relevant performance metrics for a given context. For both the PLBF and Pro-

teus, we consider the tradeoff between the filter’s False-Positive Rate (FPR) and memory footprint,

while for the MQSSD model, we consider latency and throughput. Even when using a machine-

learning model, it is still key to formalize how the model’s output relates to the relevant metric. In

the PLBF, the machine-learning model predicts whether a key is a member of a given set and out-

puts a corresponding score. To efficiently leverage this context, we formalize the relationship be-

tween these scores, the design of the backup filters, and the overall FPR. Proteus leverages a different

type of model to a similar end. Rather than using a machine learning model, the CPFPR model di-

rectly relates the design space of prefix-based range filters to their expected FPR. We demonstrate

how to leverage this context using an algorithm that efficiently navigates the design space based on

a provided workload sample and instantiates the optimal design for that use case. In contrast, the

MQSSD model is a more general framework for analyzing storage algorithms designed for modern

hardware. The MQSSD model describes the performance-critical aspects of modern SSDs in terms

of how software interacts with the hardware, namely, the number and order of page accesses, the

type of operation being executed, and the level of concurrency being used. We then use this model

to tune an example storage engine, RocksDB60, to leverage the capabilities of modern hardware

more effectively.

A.4 Additional Considerations

A.4.1 Sandwiching: A Special Case

We show here that the sandwiching approach can be interpreted as a special case of our method. In

the sandwiching approach, the learned model is sandwiched between two Bloom filters as shown in

Fig.A.1 A. The input first goes through a Bloom filter, and the negatives are discarded. The positives

are passed through the learned model where, based on their score s(x), they are either directly ac-

cepted when s(x) > t or passed through another backup Bloom filter when s(x) ≤t. In our setting,

we note that the pre-filter in the sandwiching approach can be merged with the backup filters to

yield backup filters with a modified false positive rate. Figure A.1B shows what an equivalent design

with modified false positive rates would look like. (Here, equivalence means we obtain the same false

positive rate with the same bit budget; we do not consider compute time.) Thus, the sandwiching

approach can be viewed as a special case of the PLBF with two regions.

However, this also tells us we can make the PLBF more efficient by sandwiching. Specifically,

when constructing a PLBF with k regions, if we find that fi < 1 for all i, we may assign f0 =

max1≤i≤k fi. We may then use an initial Bloom filter with a false-positive rate of f0 and change the

target false-positive rates for all other intervals to fi/f0 while keeping the same memory budget. This

approach will be somewhat more efficient computationally, as we avoid computing the learned

model for some fraction of non-key elements.

## B

## Self-Designing Range Filters

B.1 Variable Length Keys

Database workloads commonly include variable length keys, often arising from various metadata

concatenations28? . This section shows how Proteus can be used with variable-length keys and

demonstrates that the CPFPR model extends to any key length. We also show that Proteus reduces

end-to-end query latency in RocksDB by as much as 5.3x vs. SuRF on a real-world string dataset.

108


<!-- Page 119 -->


B.1.1 Extending the Model and Filter

Modeling: Shifting from a fixed length integer key space to a variable length key space in the CPFPR

model is equivalent to changing the total ordering from a less-than-or-equal relation to a lexico-

graphical relation. Proteus also has more potential designs for longer keys due to the more extensive

range of prefix lengths. In the context of static filters, the size of the longest key in the dataset is

known; therefore, Proteus’s design space is well-defined.

Filter Operation: The trie portion of Proteus handles string keys without requiring modifications.

On the other hand, variable length keys give rise to an exploding number of prefixes to query in the

prefix Bloom filters. In addition, every Bloom filter query increases the probability of a false positive.

Proteus achieves low FPR and query time by padding short keys and queries with trailing null bytes

to a chosen prefix length, thus mapping the key space onto a fixed-length key space. This means

that the prefix Bloom filter does not distinguish between short keys and their padded equivalents,

which will result in false positives if the application does not make the same assumption. Finally,

we changed the Bloom filter hash function from MurmurHash3 to CLHASH, which can handle

strings13,76.

B.1.2 Validation and Evaluation

Experimental Setup: We run in-memory and RocksDB benchmarks similar to Section 3.4.2 and

Section 3.5.3 respectively. For in-memory experiments, we generate three datasets of fixed-length

string keys of size 80, 200, and 1440 that conform to either a Uniform or Normal distribution.

Uniform keys are concatenations of uniformly generated key bytes up to the specified key length,

while Normal keys are normally distributed around the middle of the key space with standard

deviation σ = 0.01 · 264. Specifically, the mean key is defined as the string with the most signif-

icant byte value of 128, followed by null bytes up to the key length. We also generated Uniform,

are incurred at construction time and are not measured in the read-only experiment.

FPR is Unaffected by Key Length: In Figure B.1a-d, we present in-memory results for 1440-bit

keys. As with integers, Proteus outperforms SuRF across distributions and filter sizes. Experiments

with other key lengths show the same performance patterns since the primary performance factors

are the range size and key-query proximity.

Modeling Time Increases with Key Length: While the modeling accuracy is preserved across key

lengths, the number of possible designs is O(k2) with respect to the maximum key length. Longer

110


<!-- Page 121 -->


keys can, therefore, significantly increase the time required to model the designs. In our in-memory

benchmarks, the time to model all possible designs with 1440-bit keys ranged from 2.82 to 149 sec-

onds. The worst case is too expensive for most real-world applications; however, we can achieve an

order of magnitude speedup by using a coarser search as the difference in performance for similar

designs is often relatively small. The results for Proteus shown in Figure B.1 were obtained by only

modeling 128 uniformly spaced Bloom filter prefix lengths for all feasible trie depths. The modeling

times with this optimization ranged from 0.86 to 14.3 seconds while still achieving similar perfor-

mance.

The structure of the modeling also lends itself very well to parallel computation. As shown in

Section 3.3.3, the dominant cost of the sampling is extracting the information needed to model each

sample query relative to each design. This can be done independently on both a per-query and per-

design basis. Since modern database services are hosted on elastic cloud architectures, occasional

increases in CPU usage can easily be amortized at a low cost compared to the benefits of a more

performant filter.

Proteus Maintains Strong Performance on Strings: Figure B.1e shows the results of our real-

world string benchmark in RocksDB. Using the aforementioned coarse-grained modeling, Proteus

outperforms SuRF in end-to-end latency and FPR by an even greater margin. We see the impact of

design tradeoffs amplified for longer keys —SuRF’s rigid design requires a large minimum memory

budget and limits the effectiveness of additional filter memory. Conversely, Proteus’s flexible de-

sign allows it to distribute memory between its design elements for more efficient memory use. As

shown in Figure B.1e, SuRF requires at least 16 BPK, while Proteus can achieve significant perfor-

mance gains with as little as 8 BPK.
